item.title: Stochastic dengue outbreak modeling and study using nonlinear analytical techniques
item.description: arXiv:2610.38444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the present challenges of dengue outbreak is the real data driven modeling of the disease transmission dynamics which can capture the complex dynamical characteristics for accurate prediction and control. However, the conventional validation of such model is primarily based on statistical agreement between model simulated and reported incidence trajectories. In this work, we propose a seasonally driven stochastic dengue transmission model which is the modified stochastic version of the deterministic SEIR-SEI dengue outbreak model. The simulation of the proposed model is done using classical stochastic simulation algorithm. Then, the model validation is done by comparing these simulated data with the reported laboratory confirmed dengue incidence data at Imphal West district, Manipur for the three consecutive years (2023-2025) by systematic analysis using various nonlinear dynamical validation techniques. The model's performance is evaluated using coefficient of determination and relative error (RE), followed by sensitivity analysis to assess parameter robustness. The calibrated model successfully reproduces the reported outbreak trajectories for all the three years, achieving coefficients of determination greater than 0.96 and relative error less than 7%. The sensitivity analysis reveals that the transmission activation time is the most important transmission modulation parameter influencing calibration performance. Both the complexity-entropy and recurrence analyses show that the calibrated stochastic model captures substantial features of the temporal organization of the reported outbreak while retaining measurable significant differences in higher-order dynamical measures and providing complimentary information beyond conventional goodness of fit measures and offer a more comprehensive framework for validating stochastic epidemic models.
item.dc:creator: Tongbram Surkumar Singh, Mairembam Kelvin Singh, R. K. Brojen Singh, Moirangthem Shubhakanta Singh

item.title: Inferring cell property distributions from high-throughput measurement data with cell-to-cell variability
item.description: arXiv:2610.39772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-throughput measurements of cell populations produce broad distributions of observables due to inherent cell-to-cell variability. While these distributions contain valuable biological information, extracting the underlying distributions of cellular properties remains challenging. We introduce the likelihood functional, a statistical framework that infers cell property distributions by combining experimental data with deterministic computational models. The method first evaluates the model on a discrete parameter grid. Optimization of the likelihood functional is then possible without repeated model evaluations and yields best-fit property distributions which enable the direct prediction of observable distributions for comparison with experiments. As a demonstration, we apply the framework to real-time deformability cytometry data and infer cytosol and membrane viscosity distributions of human red blood cells.
item.dc:creator: Stephan Gekle

item.title: Hyaluronic acid over-expression drives tissue architecture in both healthy and diseased states
item.description: arXiv:2610.40634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tissue architecture is shaped by a variety of biomechanical and biochemical mechanisms, including morphogen patterning, differential growth, and spatial variations in cellular contractility. These mechanisms typically emphasize forces generated within cells. Here, we explore a complementary mechanism in which intercellular space itself exerts forces that shape tissue architecture. More specifically, we focus on hyaluronic acid (HA), a glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, that draws fluid into the spaces between cells through osmotic pressure, allowing these spaces to expand and mechanically deform the surrounding tissue. We propose that spatial patterning of HA-mediated extracellular forces, acting together with tissue geometry and junctional mechanics, provides a common physical framework capable of generating distinct tissue architectures. We test this hypothesis using a computational framework coupling a cell-based extended vertex model for biological tissues to a flow network representing HA and extracellular fluid in the extracellular space. This coupled model demonstrates a range of architectural responses spanning changes in tissue topology and morphology: global HA overexpression drives fluid accumulation and cell-cell junction rupture to produce multiple lumens in nontrivial patterns; a localized HA-rich region generates pressure gradients that drive budding; {\it multiple localized HA-rich regions generate branching;} and {\it extended HA-rich patterns can drive tubular structures.} Our results have direct experimental implications and establish the spatial patterning of HA-mediated intercellular forces as a mechanical morphogen helping shape tissue architecture.
item.dc:creator: Kyungeun Kim, Brittany E. Schutrum, Claudia Fischbach, J. M. Schwarz

item.title: Dual function of plasma-activated water in lettuce: growth promoter and nitrogen source under nitrogen-sufficient/-deprived conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.37742v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma generates reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) that dissolve in water, forming plasma-activated water (PAW) and inducing complex chemical changes and biological responses. PAW, enriched with nitrogen (N) species, emerges as a sustainable alternative to fertilizers by combining signaling (ROS) and N supplementation (RNS). This study investigates the dual role of PAW in lettuce, Lactuca sativa (cv. Matilda), grown under either N-sufficient or N-deprived half-strength Hoagland solutions. Four treatments were evaluated: control, seed priming in PAW-activated Hoagland, PAW-activated Hoagland cultivation, and the combination of the latter two, under both N-content regimes. Under N-sufficient conditions, seed priming in PAW increased lettuce head fresh weight by up to 40%, chlorophyll a+b by 25%, and sensory scores (freshness and juiciness) compared with the control. Under N-deprived conditions, PAW partially compensated for N deficiency, increasing plant growth by up to 50%, photosynthetic pigments and quercetin by up to 20%, and antioxidant enzyme activities (e.g., APX and G-POX increased up to 2-fold). Principal component analysis confirmed N content as the primary driver of variance (PC1, 69-71%), with PAW modulating redox homeostasis in a tissue-specific manner. Our results demonstrate the capacity of PAW to enhance plant growth, metabolism, and quality even under N-deprived conditions, addressing key gaps in plasma agriculture by highlighting the nutritional and signaling contributions of PAW. PAW therefore represents a promising and environmentally friendly strategy.
item.dc:creator: Adriana Misuthova, Zuzana Lukavcova, Ramin Mehrabifard, Zdenko Machala

item.title: Kinetics, Proofreading, and the Lifetime of Multivalent Contacts
item.description: arXiv:2610.38394v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Selective recognition is how a cell finds the right partner in a crowd and how a drug carrier finds the right cell, so getting it wrong means a missed target or a toxic one. It must also be reversible: a cell has to hold its target tightly enough to tell it from everything else, then release it to act again, and equilibrium binding, which weighs only how favorable a contact is, cannot do both. What settles recognition is how long a contact lasts. We make lifetime the control variable, passing from a master equation through a Smoluchowski equation to the Kramers lifetime of a multivalent contact. Lifetimes are exponential in free energy, so a tenfold change in receptor number moves a contact from seconds to months, turning a smooth thermodynamic gradient into a switch. Selectivity then depends on the encounter: under flow a nanoparticle is kept only if its contact outlives the vascular dwell time, which sharpens the density threshold beyond equilibrium binding. Receptor-mediated endocytosis is itself a kinetic-proofreading cascade, so uptake inherits the Kramers exponential raised to the number of driven steps, a double amplification that vanishes without metabolism and gives a testable route to phenotype-selective delivery. The same readout, on a single bond, is how a T cell discriminates antigen, with immune memory lowering the activation threshold while leaving the specificity untouched.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Battaglia

item.title: Extraordinary stiffening and reciprocal control in a DNA condensate/actin composite
item.description: arXiv:2610.38504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Soft composites, materials consisting of inclusions within a polymeric matrix, offer a broad design space with diverse mechanical properties. Composite stiffness is normally set by the volume fraction of filler, and classical theory predicts at most ~25% stiffening when inclusions occupy 10% of the volume. Here we introduce a composite of phase-separated DNA droplets that occupy <10% of an entangled actin network, yet stiffen it 25-fold, reversibly. Microscopy reveals that actin penetrates the DNA droplets, leading network elasticity to determine their size; thus the system exhibits reciprocal control between matrix and droplet properties. We attribute the extraordinary stiffening to entrainment of actin by the droplets, which enlarges the effective inclusions until their contact network dominates the mechanics. This shows that liquid-liquid phase separation can control not only local compositions, but also mechanics, achieving exceptional stiffening at modest filler fractions through local geometries that constrain the matrix beyond the inclusions themselves.
item.dc:creator: Sam Wilken, Austin Hopkins, Kyu Hwan Choi, John Berezney, Matthew E. Helgeson, M. Cristina Marchetti, Sho Takatori, Zvonimir Dogic, Omar A. Saleh

item.title: The Mean First-Reaction Time on a Thin Filament in a 3-D Domain
item.description: arXiv:2610.38715v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the mean first-reaction time (MFRT) of a Brownian particle in a bounded three-dimensional domain $\Omega$ with a reflecting boundary $\partial\Omega$, that contains a thin reactive filament. The filament is a tube of cross-sectional diameter $\varepsilon\ll 1$ around a smooth closed curve $\Gamma$, and its surface is partially reactive with reactivity $b$. As $\varepsilon\to 0$ the filament reduces to a line source in the outer problem. Its cross-section enters only through a logarithmic reactive capacitance $d_c(b)$, so that the MFRT is $\mathcal{O}(-\log[\varepsilon d_c])$. This contrasts with the $\mathcal{O}(\eps^{-1})$ scaling for spatially localized traps of radius $\eps$. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive a Fredholm integral equation on $\Gamma$ for the line density of the reactive flux. It sums all powers of $\nu\equiv -1/\log[\varepsilon d_c]$ and involves two geometric quantities: the regular part $R$ of the Neumann Green's function, which encodes the interaction of $\Gamma$ with $\partial\Omega$, and an intrinsic self-energy of $\Gamma$ that depends only on its shape. The framework extends to multiple filaments, splitting probabilities, a spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, and the principal eigenvalue of the Laplacian. For the unit sphere we solve the integral equation with a simple trapezoidal Nystr\"om scheme, and we validate the predictions for rings, linked rings and torus knots against full 3-D finite-element solutions.
item.dc:creator: Denis S. Grebenkov, Theodore Kolokolnikov, Alan E. Lindsay, Michael J. Ward

item.title: Two faces of symmetry match in gear-like coupled rotary motors
item.description: arXiv:2610.39121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rotary molecular motors commonly couple components with different rotational symmetries, but how this gearing controls energy transduction remains unclear. Here we show that symmetry can produce a fundamental tradeoff in coupled stochastic barrierless rotary motors: the gear ratio that maximizes output power under tight coupling is also the ratio that requires the strongest coupling to remain locked. Consequently, weakening the coupling can invert the effect of gearing, transforming a power maximum into a local minimum. At strong driving, both the power-optimal and most slip-susceptible ratios approach symmetry match. Numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck dynamics for rotors with finite energy barriers reproduce these predictions and reveal how the behavior changes when driving strength is fixed per rotation or per subunit. Motivated by the bacterial flagellar motor, these results identify coupling strength as a key determinant of whether matched rotational symmetries enhance or suppress energy transduction, providing a general design principle for coupled molecular motors.
item.dc:creator: Sara Iranbakhsh, David A. Sivak

item.title: Fluctuation-dissipation relation in branching particle systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.39624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A fluctuation-dissipation relation (FDR) for branching particle systems is derived that reveals how fluctuations in clonal populations originating from a single ancestor encode both population growth and the dissipative structure of the single-particle dynamics. For particles whose internal states evolve according to a stationary Markov process, the FDR holds in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium stationary states. It yields an upper bound on the spectral gap that is constrained by the magnitude of clonal fluctuations and implies that clonal dynamics is asymptotically dominated by the slowest modes of the single-particle dynamics. This provides a theoretical explanation for the persistence of clonal memory and for experimentally observed clonal cofluctuations between variables with zero covariance in the single-particle stationary state. In nonequilibrium stationary states, the FDR predicts oscillatory clonal fluctuations, suggesting a route to measuring nonequilibrium fluxes in proliferating cell populations without single-cell tracking.
item.dc:creator: Tom Michoel

item.title: Spontaneous Mutations from Terahertz Proton Tunneling
item.description: arXiv:2305.05624v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Protons in the bonds between base pairs of the double helix store the code of life by breaking the dyad symmetry that swaps the sense strand with its complementary partner. When these bonds break during replication and transcription, pairs of protons switch sides, restoring dyad symmetry and destroying genetic information. The observed rate of such spontaneous mutations is obtained in the sudden approximation for bond breaking provided protons in bonds between bases tunnel across the gap with terahertz frequency.
item.dc:creator: Noah Bray-Ali

item.title: Decoding cell signaling via optimal transport and information theory
item.description: arXiv:2602.18028v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cellular signal processing performs reliably despite molecular noise. Mutual information (MI) is widely used to quantify signaling fidelity, capturing how well outputs discriminate input states. However, it fails to capture whether the output preserves the statistical structure of the input, a property crucial in morphogen patterning and dose-dependent signaling. To address this gap, we introduce the 2-Wasserstein (2-WD) distance, which provides a geometric basis for comparing input and output distributions. We define MI as informational fidelity (INF) and the inverse of the 2-WD as geometric fidelity (GMF). Applying this dual-fidelity framework to canonical regulatory motifs under Gaussian channel approximation reveals topology-dependent trade-offs: coherent feed-forward loops can perform well in both dimensions, whereas feedback architectures reduce INF to enhance GMF. Experimental analysis of tumor necrosis factor signaling reveals dual-fidelity behavior qualitatively consistent with feedback regulation. RAS-MAPK data analysis further shows that jointly considering INF and GMF better characterizes intracellular signal relay than INF alone. Our results thus indicate that these signaling behaviors are not fully characterized by MI alone; instead, distributional correspondence provides a complementary dimension of signaling fidelity. Our study provides a practical framework for analyzing natural networks and guiding the design of task-specific synthetic circuits.
item.dc:creator: Mintu Nandi, Sosuke Ito

item.title: Active morphodynamics of intracellular organelles in the trafficking pathway
item.description: arXiv:2409.19084v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: From the Golgi apparatus to endosomes, organelles in the endomembrane system exhibit complex and varied morphologies that are often related to their function. These membrane-bound organelles operate far from equilibrium due to directed fluxes of trafficking vesicles, yet the physical principles governing the emergence and maintenance of these morphologies remain elusive. By coarse-graining the active mechanochemical cycles associated with individual fission and fusion events, we show how vesicular trafficking manifests at the hydrodynamic scale, generating not only fluxes of membrane area and encapsulated volume but also active stresses that mediate momentum transfer between an organelle and its cytosolic environment. The fluid and deformable nature of the bounding membrane gives rise to novel physics by coupling these nonequilibrium forces to organelle composition, morphology, and hydrodynamic flows. We demonstrate how both stable compartment drift and ramified sac-like morphologies, reminiscent of Golgi cisternal motion and shape, emerge from the same nonequilibrium dynamics of fission and fusion.
item.dc:creator: S. Alex Rautu, Richard G. Morris, Madan Rao

item.title: Fast projections of two-dimensional light patterns using acousto-optical deflectors
item.description: arXiv:2604.19421v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Precise and flexible control of structured light fields is essential for applications ranging from optical trapping and quantum simulation to microscopy and materials processing. Acousto-optical deflectors (AODs) are widely used in these settings due to their high speed, large damage threshold, and ability to generate steerable optical tweezers. Multi-tone driving offers a powerful alternative to slow sequential scanning, enabling the projection of complex patterns with high accuracy as rapid acoustic modulation averages out inter-spot interference. In two dimensions, however, intermodulation between tones in orthogonal AODs can reintroduce coherent artifacts. We present a fast, feedback-free AOD projection scheme based on an incommensurately staggered frequency lattice that intrinsically suppresses such artifacts. For separable two-dimensional target patterns, our method removes the need for scanning entirely, enabling substantially faster and highly accurate projections. We further extend the approach to non-separable images using a minimal scanning strategy that maintains rather high projection speeds. These results demonstrate that appropriately engineered multi-tone AOD driving offers an efficient and robust route to high-speed, high-fidelity generation of arbitrary intensity patterns.
item.dc:creator: Robbert Decruyenaere, Clara Tanghe, Senne Van Wellen, Karel Van Acoleyen

item.title: Hybrid Dynamical Simulation Reveals Apparent Stiffening of Flexible Protein Lattices Driving Membrane Bending
item.description: arXiv:2607.06378v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Membrane-deforming protein lattices play a central role in essential and pathogenic remodeling processes, including clathrin-mediated endocytosis and viral budding. Simulating these systems at biologically relevant length and time scales requires mesoscale approaches that preserve structural detail. We present a hybrid simulation framework that couples a particle-based flexible protein lattice to a continuum membrane model, enabling systematic investigation of how lattice geometry and rigidity influence membrane remodeling. We validate the coupled model by comparing simulation results with theoretical predictions for membranes under increasing tension. Using buckling-based deformations of pre-assembled clathrin lattices, we quantify the lattice flexural rigidity and establish a direct relationship between the force constants in the coarse-grained energy function and the emergent lattice mechanics. We then compare this flexural rigidity, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{flex}}$, to an effective rigidity, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{eff}}$, commonly used in continuum descriptions of sphere-forming protein assemblies. Although $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{flex}}$ is set solely by the energy function, $\kappa_{l,\mathrm{eff}}$ depends on lattice size and connectivity, with the two measures converging for weakly-connected lattices. As a result, with lattice growth, the effective rigidity relevant for spherical bud formation increases and the relaxation timescale decreases. This size-dependent stiffening highlights the importance of structural details in interpreting lattice mechanics and cautions against assuming a single constant stiffness. We demonstrate the generality of the method by applying it to pre-assembled viral lattices generated with reaction-diffusion simulations. This work provides a validated framework for simulating deformable protein assemblies of diverse geometry coupled to membrane dynamics and remodeling.
item.dc:creator: Samuel L. Foley, Margaret E. Johnson

item.title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
item.description: arXiv:2607.16517v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.
item.dc:creator: Eve Bodnia, Margaux Basart, Sofie Hai, Lenzie Ford, Nina Miolane, Kenneth S. Kosik, Dirk Bouwmeester, Lincoln D. Carr

item.title: The limits of higher-order interactions in shaping chimera states
item.description: arXiv:2610.31997v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In neuronal networks, chimera states, characterized by the coexistence of coherent and incoherent populations, have attracted considerable attention in the study of collective brain dynamics, due to its potential implications for neurological disorders such as epilepsy. Their emergence has been extensively investigated with a particular emphasis on the role of network topology, both in conventional pairwise interactions and, more recently, in higher-order interaction networks. Here, we propose a generalized framework for neuronal hypergraphs incorporating higher-order interactions through attractive chemical and repulsive electrical coupling. Using networks of FitzHugh--Nagumo neurons with interaction orders d=2,3,4, corresponding to (d+1)-body interactions within a framework that can be extended to higher d, we numerically investigate the emergence of chimera states under the combined effect of attractive and repulsive coupling and we compare the resulting dynamics with those of their corresponding clique-projected networks. Our results reveal that, both dynamical similarities and qualitative differences between genuine higher-order interactions on hypergraphs and their pairwise representations. While higher-order interactions often support broader chimera regions, we show that clique projections can also preserve or promote chimera states, even in regimes where the corresponding hypergraphs exhibit fully incoherent dynamics. Therefore, these findings suggest that chimera formation is not only influenced by the topology or by the interaction order but also by the form of the coupling functions and the balance between attractive and repulsive interactions, offering further insights into collective dynamics in neuronal networks.
item.dc:creator: Ediline L. F. Nguessap, Thierry Njougouo, Fernando Fagundes Ferreira
